title: Creole society and where Lewis grew up in the Creole section
summary: Lewis describes Creole social attitudes about hiring musicians and the streets, including St. Claude, where he lived until grown.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: What about now these people you associate with the Creole kind of music like Piku and the big guy, Lillian Nelson and so on. Did they all tend to play in one area of town like in the downhill?

No, I don't think so. I'll tell you about the Creole people in the audience was like this one. Put a little Espinay Street. Uh. From Seminole. I said Seminole. Going back to Broad. I said from Clayborne. Uh. Columbus Valley. Well. There were different kinds of people. Because they thought they were more important than the, the poor, the poor, the other guy. You see. So they, uh. Many times they would not hire others to talk with the citizens. Uh. But, uh. They would hire a leader of Abraham. He had a great, uh, right skin. Then they would have to play with him. But they said hire me persons, it wouldn't do it.
Uh huh. Actually you lived very much in that, uh, in that Creole section, didn't you?

I had been, but not as far back as that. I lived, uh, St. Claude, Espinay, and Calvary. He was a bishop, a Catholic bishop. Bishop, uh, Frank. Bishop Frank. Uh. He lived in this big house. There was a Catholic nuns on that farm. But I stood in that neighborhood. Uh. And I was a man in that chair. He said, uh. I wanted the first I ever lived out of the Creole section. He was here. Okay. Okay. The first back on the Orleans I ever lived was Prid Street. And we only stood there for a short time. I was removed to, as the grandmother died, it was St. Claude Street. And I stood there until I was a man. And the first front, from that time on, I lived it was St. Claude, uh, eight, uh, eight, 27 St. Claude. And I lived it right from the, uh, one block from the old Globes, or Globes, or Globes. And it was a Globes all. Okay.
But anyway, now, would you agree that there were different, that there were different styles of playing, but then that it wasn't necessary in different areas of the city?
